::: {#sol-bikeshare-histogram}

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

##### R

```{r}
#| code-fold: show
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Histogram of the number of bikes rented per hour.
#|   The tallest bars are at the smallest counts,
#|   and the bars shrink steadily toward a long thin tail
#|   that reaches the largest counts.
bikeshare_raw |>
  ggplot2::ggplot() +
  ggplot2::aes(x = bikers) +
  ggplot2::geom_histogram(bins = 30) + # check-unexplained-choices: allow
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Bikes rented in the hour", y = "Number of hours")
```

##### Python

```{python}
#| code-fold: show
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Histogram of the number of bikes rented per hour.
#|   The tallest bars are at the smallest counts,
#|   and the bars shrink steadily toward a long thin tail
#|   that reaches the largest counts.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4), layout="constrained")
ax.hist(bikeshare_raw["bikers"], bins=30);  # check-unexplained-choices: allow
ax.set_xlabel("Bikes rented in the hour");
ax.set_ylabel("Number of hours");
plt.show()
```

:::

```{r}
#| include: false
bikers_median <- median(bikeshare_raw$bikers)
hours_per_bin <- nrow(bikeshare_raw) / 30
hours_per_bin_round <- round(hours_per_bin)
```

I chose 30 bars,
which is about `r hours_per_bin_round` hours per bar.
Far fewer bars would hide the long right tail inside a few wide bars,
and far more would leave most bars with only a few hours,
so the outline would look ragged.

The [histogram](exploratory-descriptive.qmd#def-histogram) is right-skewed:
the [sample median](exploratory-descriptive.qmd#def-sample-median) of `bikers` is `r bikers_median`,
below its [sample mean](exploratory-descriptive.qmd#def-sample-mean) of `r bikers_mean_round`.
Counts cannot be negative,
and nothing caps them,
which is the situation that a [Poisson regression model](poisson-regression.qmd#def-poisson-regression) is built for.

:::
